La COVID-19 n’épargne personne. Tandis q: COVID-19 spares no one. As everyone is told to stay home, we must remember that people experiencing homelessness don’t have that luxury. How is the pandemic affecting this forgotten population? And how will they cope with the curfew? Those living the crisis up close speak out. Starting tomorrow, it will be illegal to be out on the streets of Quebec from 8 p.m. to 5 a.m. The consequences of breaking the curfew will be severe: offenders will face a steep fine of $1,000 to $6,000.
Le premier ministre François Legault ne: Premier François Legault does not plan to make any exception for people experiencing homelessness. “There are places set aside. What we obviously want, with the cold, is for them to be indoors; and there are enough spaces,” he said at a press conference. When asked about this, the premier’s office maintains that there are currently enough spaces available to meet needs, adding that actions are under way with community organizations and the City of Montréal. The story is different, however, among services and shelters, which say emergency services are already overloaded and there aren’t enough spaces available. Nakuset, who runs the Native Women’s Shelter of Montréal, sees a serious problem here.
« Vous allez leur donner des contraventi: “Are you going to give them tickets or ignore them? Either way, it doesn’t work,” she says. “You can’t make people who live on the street ‘stay home’ if you haven’t given them anything. If there are 4,000 homeless people, we need 4,000 beds,” she says. According to the latest counts, 3,150 people were experiencing homelessness in Montréal in 2018. That number has most likely risen considerably since then. Only 1,526 spaces will be available for people experiencing homelessness, according to the City of Montréal, which says it is working “in concert with the SPVM, the health network and community organizations to support and assist vulnerable people with an approach of tolerance and compassion.”
Du côté du Service de police de la Ville: As for the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM), there is still no concrete action plan for enforcing these measures among people experiencing homelessness on the eve of the curfew. “A preventive and adapted approach will be favoured,” the SPVM’s media relations office simply told us. For people experiencing homelessness, the COVID outbreak and the curfew are factors that worsen their already precarious situation.
David Chapman et Joyce Méus, à l’accueil: David Chapman and Joyce Méus at the front desk of Résilience, a day shelter Photo: Christelle Saint-Julien
Cette précarité se fait sentir dans les: This precarity is felt in the shelters, which now have to deal with a major new problem. “If there’s an outbreak here, we could have to close at any moment,” says David Chapman, coordinator of Résilience Montréal, a shelter for people experiencing homelessness. The threat is very real: a catastrophic rise in COVID-19 cases forced the temporary closure of La Porte ouverte, another shelter, last December. Near downtown, numerous infections have also been recorded at the Projets Autochtones du Québec (PAQ) shelter. While staff at Résilience Montréal are on a war footing, good spirits prevail there too.
À l’entrée, les intervenants accueillent: At the entrance, the support workers greet clients with hand sanitizer and a thermometer, and offer them face coverings. People can no longer linger, rest in the shelter, or even chat at length with the workers. Inside, no more than 12 visitors are admitted at a time. “They come to get food and clothing from behind a plexiglass window. Then they go right back outside, into the cold,” the shelter’s coordinator explains sadly. “Some people have a hard time with this rigidity. But we explain that we have no choice,” adds Mr. Chapman. “We want to treat people with respect and dignity, but with these measures, it’s impossible.” Instead of carrying out its usual activities, the staff is focusing its efforts elsewhere.
« Le véritable enjeu de sécurité, c’est: “The real safety issue is that they have a shelter,” says Joyce, who works as a support worker. Her role is to help Résilience’s clients access housing and to offer them support. After the rise in infections, every appointment on her schedule was cancelled. “I understand that this is an emergency,” she acknowledges. What she fears most is that the relationship she has with her clients will suffer. “I spend an enormous amount of time helping them look, to earn their trust. I’m really afraid that this whole relationship, that the trust will be broken.” Near the shelter, at the corner of Atwater and Sainte-Catherine streets, we meet Mike.
« Les gens commencent à être confus. Que: “People are starting to get confused. What are we supposed to do?” asks the young man, who lives on the street. “Everything keeps changing, people are confused,” he says, referring to the measures and the services available. “Not everyone has somewhere to go. Now the shelters are closed, and people can’t go sleep. And I know there are a lot of people who have to isolate,” Mike explains. “People are getting chased away, and things aren’t going to get better,” the man in his thirties continues shyly. “There were a lot of us here before – a lot of Inuit, a lot of Indigenous people. Now there are only a handful of us.”
Il croit que plusieurs des gens de sa co: He believes that many of the people he knew have died, unless they found housing or left the city to return to their communities. “Since the coronavirus, we’re constantly being hassled,” he says, pointing to the metro station and the Alexis Nihon shopping centre.

À quelques rues de Résilience, on croise: A few blocks from Résilience, we come across Franky, who is currently staying at Chez Doris, a shelter for women experiencing homelessness. The 53-year-old mother lost her job as a building caretaker last October. She had just lost her mother, who died of cancer. A fractured shoulder on December 13 then kept her from going back to work. Unshakable, Franky nonetheless stays positive. Her attitude is contagious; she makes us laugh throughout the hour we spend with her. Only recently homeless, she hopes the current situation will at least draw attention to what homeless and vulnerable people are going through. “I’ve fought a lot of battles, and here’s the next one: homelessness, and the way people are treated.”
« Être itinérant, c’est beaucoup de trav: “Being homeless is a lot of work, especially with the lockdown in a red zone,” she confides. “Every day, we have to leave the premises for an hour so the cleaning can be done. Normally we can go to the mall for an hour. Now, as soon as we go in, security guards tell us we can’t stay there. We can’t go eat at McDonald’s for an hour and come back either. Everything is closed, where are we supposed to go?” she pleads. You have to stay outside. Warming centres aren’t as easy to access since the outbreaks this winter.
Chez Doris, où on accueille en moyenne 7: At Chez Doris, which welcomes an average of 70 women experiencing homelessness every day, the facility’s capacity has been reduced in line with safety measures. Currently, only 40 women can be inside because of physical distancing measures. Originally a day shelter, the organization has been able to extend its opening hours and has offered overnight accommodation since December 1. The outbreaks in neighbouring shelters worry management. “There’s a percentage of the homeless population that’s positive right now, and it could get worse,” believes Marina Boulos-Winton, director of Chez Doris. “When a shelter closes, it takes a resource away from the community.”
Si l’organisme a évité le pire pour l’in: While the organization has avoided the worst so far, the situation remains worrying. “I’ve only had one case of COVID among employees, but I had to take eight people off work,” says Ms. Boulos-Winton. The temporary absence of these employees forced the shelter to reorganize its activities, and it had to outsource certain services to fill the gap.
« La santé publique nous a dit de ne pas: “Public health told us not to accept new women,” says the director of Chez Doris. “We don’t know whether someone coming into our bubble will contaminate something. We try to direct women elsewhere or, if they’re newly homeless, we take them in,” she explains. Above all, she wants people experiencing homelessness to avoid going to different places for services. “We don’t want women going from shelter to shelter. They now have to choose one shelter and keep using the same one.”
Interrogée par La Converse, la Ville de: When asked by La Converse, the City of Montréal said it is supporting community organizations across the various resources to ensure services continue. But Ms. Boulos-Winton believes the measures put in place by the City are not adapted to the reality of people experiencing homelessness. If one of them shows symptoms of COVID-19, they are generally directed to the Hôtel-Dieu clinic to get tested.
Les personnes en attente de leurs résult: People awaiting their results are then directed to “orange zone” services so they can isolate. Those who test positive are sent to a “red zone” to be treated and isolated. Spaces are limited, and the facilities are running at full capacity. “For people experiencing homelessness, it’s very hard to isolate, unless they’re offered a room for the whole day. But not everyone can stay in their room,” explains Ms. Boulos-Winton. “They have to keep using the resources they need.”
Selon la directrice, le va-et-vient des: According to the director, people going back and forth between different services contributes to the spread of the virus, especially if those people are infected. “There aren’t enough services for people who use drugs, so they wander around and infect others,” she believes. The PAQ shelter, which serves the Indigenous community, is one of the few facilities that offer this type of service. It has been identified as a hotspot for transmission.
Marina Boulos-Winton souhaite que des te: Marina Boulos-Winton wants rapid tests to be available in shelters, but also in open areas like Cabot Square, where people experiencing homelessness spend time. David Chapman agrees. “This summer, a testing site was set up at Cabot Square in collaboration with the CIUSSS,” he says. For the moment, no initiative of that kind is under way. “There’s a skating rink that almost nobody uses. A lot of money was spent to give the middle class a chance to get away from it all.
Ce qui aurait pu également être mis en p: What could also have been set up is a big tent with adequate heating where homeless people could have stayed safely, at a distance from one another.”
À la Maison du Père, qui offre plusieurs: At the Maison du Père, which offers several services, including emergency shelter, social reintegration and a residence for seniors with a history of homelessness, measures have also been tightened to prevent an outbreak. Thanks to the facility’s status, the seniors who live at the Maison du Père are regularly tested on site by medical staff.
Par contre, la clientèle qui fréquente l: However, the clients who use the shelter must go through the testing steps mentioned above. Jaëlle Begarin, director of clinical programs at the Maison du Père, wants the seriousness of the situation people experiencing homelessness find themselves in to be taken into account. “We really want public health to keep us in its priority category – for access to measures, equipment and, above all, vaccination,” she insists. “All organizations offering services to people experiencing homelessness should be on the priority list to get the vaccine, especially Indigenous organizations. If workers are vaccinated, they’ll be able to keep working,” adds Nakuset. She also wants the City to declare a state of emergency for Montréal’s shelters.
« Le gouvernement provincial aurait dû a: “The provincial government should have had an action plan, especially with winter approaching,” she believes. The director of the Native Women’s Shelter of Montréal also points out that the army, as it did in long-term care homes, could go lend a hand in shelters for people experiencing homelessness. “People experiencing homelessness could stay in heated tents monitored by members of the army. I really hope that at some point they’ll offer solutions before organizations have to close their doors. Homeless people have nothing, and now they have even less,” she concludes.
Voici donc les solutions que proposent l: These, then, are the solutions put forward by the people on the front lines. Solutions that are nothing new. Will the government listen?
We’ll see in the coming days.
